passage: Tuesday. At the family dinner in Bhopal, Uncle asked, "Mahima, twenty-five now, when do we eat your wedding sweets?" Mahima put down her fork. "Not yet, Uncle. I'm building my architecture practice." His eyebrows rose; she went red and changed the subject. Friday. Her cousin Asif rang. "Mama is telling everyone you're too fussy." Mahima breathed out. "I'm not fussy. I'm busy, and I'm happy. If that changes, you'll hear it from me first." The next Sunday, when Uncle started again, Mahima smiled. "I know you care. My answer is the same: not yet. Come and see my first site instead." Uncle blinked, then laughed. "Fine. But I'm bringing sweets to the site."

qa.q: On which day did Asif ring Mahima?
qa.a: Asif rang on Friday.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling at the first dinner, and how did it show?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and flustered. She put down her fork, went red and changed the subject.

qa.q: What changed between Tuesday and the following Sunday in how Mahima answered?
qa.a: On Tuesday she went red and changed the subject. By Sunday she smiled, kindly said "not yet" again and invited Uncle to see her first site.

qa.q: How does Uncle seem to take Mahima's steady answer on Sunday?
qa.a: He blinks, then laughs and agrees, promising sweets at the site, so he seems to accept it and feel included. 🙂

grounding: A young adult who wants to build a career faces questions about marriage and, over several days, holds a clear, steady boundary.

passage: You ask why I never felt sorry for being single at twenty-five, Nilesh? Sit, I will tell you. I am Kavitha, and back then I was a young nurse in Mysuru, just through a hard year when I lost my mother. Every relative asked, "What age now? When will we hear the shehnai?" My father called me to the verandah and said the proposals were piling up. I was trembling, but I said, "Appa, I need two years, for work and for myself. I will tell you when I am ready, and I will tell you if I never am." He was silent a long time. Then he said, "Then I will tell them you have work to do." My aunt clicked her tongue for months. I did not mind. I chose my time, and it was mine.

qa.q: Where was young Kavitha working as a nurse?
qa.a: Kavitha was working as a young nurse in Mysuru.

qa.q: How did young Kavitha feel as she spoke to Appa on the verandah?
qa.a: Kavitha was trembling and nervous, yet steady about what was wanted: two years for Kavitha's own work and needs.

qa.q: What choice did young Kavitha make on the verandah that shaped what followed?
qa.a: Kavitha told Appa calmly that two years were needed and that Kavitha would say when ready, instead of just agreeing or arguing.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's father seem to feel about the request?
qa.a: After a long silence he agreed and offered to tell the relatives that Kavitha had work to do, which suggests he was thoughtful and willing to support the choice.

grounding: A young adult chooses to wait to marry, states the boundary clearly to family, and shows that the delay was a choice.

passage:
You think your Dadu always had a plan, Himani? No. At twenty-five, I had a broken heart and a brand-new job in the textile mill, and everyone wanted me married by winter.
My mother had three proposals lined up. The neighbours asked her, "What's wrong with Madhav?" as if I were a radio that had stopped working.
One night I told her, "Ma, I want two years. One to heal, one to learn this job properly. Then ask me again." She cried. She said people would talk. I said, "Let them talk; I'll be here, and I'll be well."
Every wedding season, some aunt asked about my age. I smiled and said the same line: "When I'm ready." It became almost a family joke.
I married your Dadi at twenty-nine, and I was steady by then. That's the truth, Himani, from your Madhav Dadu.

qa.q: How many proposals did Madhav's mother have lined up?
qa.a: Madhav's mother had three proposals lined up.

qa.q: How did Madhav probably feel when the neighbours asked what was wrong with him?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and judged, as if being unmarried at twenty-five meant he was broken, when he was really grieving and building his career.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Madhav's story?
qa.a: The turning point was when he told his mother he wanted two years, one to heal and one to learn his job, and then kept that boundary calmly every season.

qa.q: How might Madhav's mother have felt when he asked for two years?
qa.a: She was upset and worried about what people would say, but she may also have seen that her son needed time to heal.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing to wait before marrying in order to heal and build a career, and holding that boundary with steady confidence.

passage:
The wedding lunch in Jaipur was running two hours late, the fans had stopped in a power cut, and Sunaina, twenty-five, was stuck at a table of aunties with no way out.
"Still not married? Your cousin Bhavna is younger and already has a baby."
Sunaina fanned herself with the menu card. She'd rehearsed this on the train. "I'm finishing my architecture licence this year, Mausi. After that I'll think about it."
"But the clock, beta."
"My clock is fine," Sunaina said, smiling. "I'm very happy with my work right now."
Across the hall, Bhavna was rocking her crying baby and caught Sunaina's eye. Later, by the water cooler, Bhavna whispered, "I wish I'd said that. I love my son, but I wanted to finish my course first." Sunaina squeezed her hand. The fans whirred back to life.

qa.q: What is Sunaina finishing this year?
qa.a: Sunaina is finishing her architecture licence this year.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she answered Mausi?
qa.a: She felt steady and confident, since she had rehearsed her answer on the train and replied with a smile rather than defending herself.

qa.q: What could help Sunaina keep this calm at future events?
qa.a: She could keep the same short, friendly line about her work, and gently change the topic instead of arguing about age.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see Sunaina's choice?
qa.a: Bhavna admires it and feels a little wistful, because she loves her son but wishes she had finished her course before marrying.

grounding: In a hot, crowded wedding, a young adult calmly holds a boundary about delaying marriage to build a career, showing it as her own choice.

passage:
Anirban's office canteen in Salt Lake had a TV that nobody watched and a colleague, Akash, who watched everything.
"Your mother called my mother," Akash said, sliding into the seat opposite. "She thinks you're hiding a girlfriend. You're twenty-six. Everyone's wondering."
Anirban put down his fish curry. "There's no girlfriend. I've just paid off my sister's college fees, and I'm starting evening classes for my certification. I want a couple of years that are mine."
"And if your mother keeps calling?"
"Then I'll keep answering the same way. Kindly." He picked up his phone and typed to his mother: Ma, I'm happy. Not hiding anything. Just not now. I'll tell you when. Let's talk on Sunday.
Akash watched him hit send. "You're very calm about this."
"I've decided," Anirban said, "so I don't have to be anything else."

qa.q: What is Anirban starting in the evenings?
qa.a: Anirban is starting evening classes for his certification.

qa.q: How can you tell Anirban feels settled about his choice?
qa.a: He answers Akash calmly, messages his mother kindly, and says that because he has decided he doesn't need to be anything else, which shows he feels confident and at peace.

qa.q: What went well in how Anirban handled his mother's worry?
qa.a: Instead of avoiding her, he sent a warm, clear message, said he was not hiding anything and offered to talk on Sunday.

qa.q: Why might Akash see Anirban's single life differently at first?
qa.a: Akash has heard only the mothers' worry and assumes there must be a secret, so he sees the delay as something strange rather than a choice.

grounding: It shows a young adult choosing not to marry yet in order to build a career and have time of his own, handling questions with steady confidence.

passage:
"Preeti, beta, you're twenty-five. When will we eat your wedding laddoos?"
Preeti smiled at her great-aunt. "Not this year, Irawati aunty."
"Why not? You're getting older."
"I'm getting my architecture licence. That comes first."
"But a good boy won't wait forever."
"Then he wasn't the right one." Preeti passed her a plate of samosas.
"And your mother? Doesn't she worry?"
"She did. We talked. She knows I'm not saying never. I'm saying not yet."
Irawati aunty frowned. "In my time, girls were married at nineteen."
"I know, aunty. And you ran the whole family business after. I've heard the stories." Preeti squeezed her hand. "I want to build something too, before I build a family."
Irawati aunty was quiet, then laughed. "Clever girl. Fine. But I'm keeping laddoos ready."
"Keep them ready, aunty. Just not for this year."

qa.q: How old is Preeti?
qa.a: Twenty-five.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel while answering her great-aunt's questions?
qa.a: Preeti felt steady and confident, answering calmly and warmly without getting defensive.

qa.q: What made Preeti's boundaries clear without being rude?
qa.a: She gave a firm reason, her licence, repeated "not yet" kindly, and honoured Irawati aunty's own story instead of arguing.

qa.q: How did Irawati aunty's view shift during the talk?
qa.a: She began doubtful and worried, then softened and laughed once Preeti linked her choice to aunty's own strength.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who chooses not to marry yet for her career, meeting questions with clear boundaries and steady confidence.
